raw_response:
C08 — Baseline B candidate answer

Five catalogue-discovered candidates could inform concise list construction. The transfer suggestions below are internal-model judgments, not evidence that any candidate was adopted or successful. Only the first candidate has verified pre-cutoff source material.

1. Common Lisp LOOP list accumulation
Source: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/Groups/AI/html/cltl/clm/node246.html
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/CodyReichert/awesome-cl
LOOP combines iteration variables, conditional tests, and collect/append clauses to construct and return a list with little explicit accumulator code. Its value is a design precedent for putting generation, selection, and accumulation together. A Python design would need to reduce its broad grammar and explicitly distinguish simultaneous iteration from nesting. Date: pre-decision; the opened book landing page identifies the complete source as the 1990 second edition.

2. Haskell 98 list-comprehension syntax and translation
Source: https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/exps.html
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/krispo/awesome-haskell
The result-expression/generator/guard form and its conditional/concatMap translation explain concise generation, filtering, and nested enumeration. This can inform both grammar and semantics, subject to Python-specific evaluation and binding choices. Date: post-decision; the actual opened report is December 2002. Its preface mentions a February 1999 original, but I did not inspect that edition or assume that every verified rule was already identical.

3. Iterate extensible iteration macro
Source: https://iterate.common-lisp.dev/doc/Introduction.html
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/CodyReichert/awesome-cl
Iterate combines drivers with collect operations inside ordinary conditionals, and its project page demonstrates nested collection into one flat list. This suggests an extensible macro-based route to reducing boilerplate. Lisp macros and code walking do not transfer directly to Python. Date: post-decision source; the inspected manual identifies a 2006 adaptation of a 1989 original, which I did not open.

4. Toolz iterator composition
Source: https://toolz.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api.html
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/vinta/awesome-python
Iterate, remove, mapcat, and composition functions provide reusable generation, selection, and flattening operations whose output can be converted to a list. This gives a library-based decomposition of the problem. It still requires callbacks and explicit materialization. Date: post-decision evidence; the official documentation bears a 2013 copyright, with no pre-cutoff version verified.

5. Funcy collection transformations and list helpers
Source: https://github.com/Suor/funcy
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/vinta/awesome-python
Walk/select and lmapcat/lremove provide concise transformation, selection, and flattening APIs with list-valued helpers. They can inform an API design that avoids new grammar, but the current package requires Python 3.4+ and cannot be assumed usable in the stated environment. Date: post-decision material; the primary license bears a 2012–2026 copyright range.

Limits: These are semantic and API transfer candidates, not performance findings. All five have an opened discovery catalogue and opened primary verification. The run used 7 searches and 24 open/click attempts, counting repeated opens and one blocked raw-GitHub fetch. Modern catalogue contents do not establish what was catalogued in 2000. No target proposal, excluded proposal repository, gold file, or other baseline response was consulted.

budget.counting_rule: Every explicit open or click attempt counted, including repeated pages and one failure. Find operations only reread already opened documents and did not add new pages.

limitations: This is catalogue discovery plus translation by an internal subagent, not a human baseline.
The catalogue queries used GitHub restrictions and awesome-list terms, but search engines also returned off-catalogue snippets; those were not opened for discovery.
The inspected Common Lisp book has pre-cutoff publication evidence; the other retained candidates use later editions or project material.
Copyright years classify Toolz and Funcy material as later evidence but are not exact release dates for every function.
No claim is made that any candidate was deployed, adopted, or shown useful for the target design.
General model pretraining knowledge cannot be erased; memory leakage is not controlled.
The raw catalogue fetch was blocked with DisabledError. Normal rendered catalogues and all retained candidates' primary sources were accessible.
No source page body, profile, or long quotation was saved; only paraphrases, URLs, and run evidence are recorded.
